topic: Walking pace vs step count: under 5,000 brisk steps matched 10,000 slow ones for mortality risk (BJSM, 100k+ UK Biobank)
angle: 'Steps AND pace: a walking cheat sheet.' In 100k+ UK Biobank adults (BJSM 2026), people who walked under 5,000 steps a day but hit a brisker peak pace (>80 steps/min) had a death risk similar to people walking 5,000–7,500 steps at a slow ~60 steps/min. 7,500–10,000 steps was linked to the lowest risk at any pace. Slides: (1) the core finding; (2) cadence guide: ~60 = leisurely, >80 = brisker (study), ~100 = moderate intensity (other research); (3) 15-second self-test: count steps ×4 to check your current pace; (4) how step count and pace combine; (5) 'observational: a link, not proof'; (6) any pace beats none, so build up gradually. Drop the 8,500-steps note unless its source is verified. Title: 'The Walking Pace Cheat Sheet: How Fast Is Fast Enough?' is fine.
title: The Walking Pace Cheat Sheet: How Fast Is Fast Enough?

topic: Stroke in younger adults: rising rates in ages 20–54 and the BE-FAST warning signs
angle: A public-service list: 'Stroke isn't just an old person's disease.' title: Stroke Before 50: The 5 Signs That Mean Call Emergency Services Now

topic: Smartwatch calorie estimates off by 15–25% vs lab gold standard, with larger errors at higher body fat (PLOS One)
angle: 'Your watch's calories-burned number is a rough estimate.' In a small lab test (58 adults, 10 minutes of cycling), 4 popular smartwatches were off by a median of about 15–25% against a lab gas-analysis gold standard. Most overestimated, and the error grew at higher body fat. It's a small, short study, so treat it as a caution, not a verdict. Watches are better at tracking trends in steps and heart rate than exact calories. Don't extrapolate weekly calorie totals and give no eating instructions. Suggested title: 'How Accurate Is Your Smartwatch's Calorie Count? A Lab Test Checked'.
title: Smartwatch Calories Were Off by 15–25% in a Lab Test #shorts

topic: HRT pills vs patches: the '1 in 1,000' absolute risk behind the blood clot headlines
angle: A Danish registry study in The BMJ (women 50–69) linked oral HRT to a higher risk of blood clots in the legs or lungs. In absolute terms that's about [paper's figure] extra clots per 1,000 women per year. Patches and gels showed no overall increase in clot risk. The likely reason is that pills pass through the liver first. It's observational, and individual risk varies. Close with: 'Ask your clinician which route fits you, and don't stop or switch on your own.'
title: HRT pill vs patch: the blood clot number headlines skip #shorts

topic: Scented cleaners + indoor ozone create billions of nanoparticles within minutes (Purdue, ACS Fall 2026)
angle: That 'fresh clean' scent comes from terpenes such as limonene and pinene, including in 'natural' essential-oil cleaners. Indoors they react with ozone, and in Purdue's house tests the tiny particles formed could deliver a lung dose similar to standing by a busy road within about 20 minutes. Three fixes: choose fragrance-free products, run an exhaust fan while cleaning, and don't use ozone-generating 'air purifiers'. Say clearly: this is early conference data, and scientists are still working out the health effects.
title: Your "clean" smell might be polluting your air #shorts
